question: Which do readers judge most accurately: the angles of pie slices, the areas of circles, or positions along one axis?
answer: Positions along one axis. In 1984 William Cleveland and Robert McGill tested how well people compare values coded in different ways: positions on a common scale came first, then lengths, angles and areas, with colour shading last. That is why dots or bars on a shared axis beat pies and bubbles.
move: To make numbers comparable, put them on one shared scale.
ask: Which pie chart have I squinted at when a row of bars would have answered?
trap: Pie slices, because a pie shows parts of a whole.
reference: William S. Cleveland and Robert McGill, Graphical Perception, Journal of the American Statistical Association 79(387):531–554, 1984
